title: Is Criminal Forensics Bullshit? - Nautilus
gist: A short teaser noting that the 'CSI effect' on jurors is real in expectation but not tied to TV viewing, and that University of British Columbia law professor Sara Gordon has found common forensic techniques such as blood pattern analysis, ballistics and drug-sniffing dogs scientifically lacking.

insights.claim: A 2008 survey of more than 2,000 jurors found they increasingly expected lab-grade scientific evidence from prosecutors, but this expectation was not linked to watching CSI-style TV shows.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Rising juror expectations for scientific evidence raise the bar and cost of prosecutions.

insights.claim: Jurors' higher evidence expectations appear driven by general awareness of advances in forensic science rather than by television, contrary to prosecutors' 'CSI effect' complaints.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Public science literacy, not media, shapes demand for evidentiary rigor.

insights.claim: Law professor Sara Gordon of the University of British Columbia published three analyses finding blood pattern analysis, ballistics and drug-sniffing dog evidence scientifically lacking despite often going unquestioned by judges.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Challenges to forensic validity could drive wrongful-conviction litigation and reform of evidence standards.
insights.quote: a trio of deep dives into a few common techniques—which often go unquestioned by judges—and found them quite lacking
